query: Which privacy-preserving record linkage approaches (Bloom filters, PSRL, cryptographic salts) are most practical given partner reluctance to share identifiers and legal DPA constraints?

response.query: Which privacy-preserving record linkage approaches (Bloom filters, PSRL, cryptographic salts) are most practical given partner reluctance to share identifiers and legal DPA constraints?
response.answer: Bloom filters are practical for privacy-preserving record linkage due to their efficiency and comparable linkage quality. Cryptographic salts and probabilistic record linkage methods also offer strong privacy protections. These approaches minimize identifier sharing, addressing partner reluctance and legal constraints.

results.content: Secure Privacy Preserving Record Linkage of Large Databases by Modified Bloom Filter Encodings - PMC An official website of the United States government Here's how you know Here's how you know A **.gov** website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. doi: 10.23889/ijpds.v1i1.29 Secure Privacy Preserving Record Linkage of Large Databases by Modified Bloom Filter Encodings ### Rainer Schnell Find articles by Rainer Schnell ### Christian Borgs 2 German Record Linkage Center - University of Duisburg-Essen Find articles by Christian Borgs 2 German Record Linkage Center - University of Duisburg-Essen Corresponding author: Rainer @uni-due.de This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. In most European settings, record linkage across different institutions has to be based on personal identifiers such as names, birthday or place of birth. In practice, these identifiers show error rates up to 20% per identifier, therefore linking on encrypted identifiers usually implies the loss of large subsets of the databases. These problems gave rise to techniques of Privacy Preserving Record Linkage (PPRL). Many different PPRL techniques have been suggested within the last 10 years, very few of them are suitable for practical applications with large database containing millions of records as they are typical for administrative or medical databases. One proven technique for PPRL for large scale applications is PPRL based on Bloom filters. Using appropriate parameter settings, Bloom filter approaches show linkage results comparable to linkage based on unencrypted identifiers. However, Bloom filters have been subject of cryptographic attacks. Previous research has shown that the straight application of Bloom filters has a nonzero re-identification risk. We will present new results on recently developed techniques to defy all known attacks on PPRL Bloom filters. results.title: Privacy-Preserving Record Linkage
results.content: Given several databases containing person-specific data held by different organizations, privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL) aims to identify and link records that correspond to the same entity/individual across different databases based on the matching of personal identifying attributes, such as name and address, without revealing the actual values in these attributes due to privacy concerns. Accepted 2021 Oct 28; Collection date 2022. ### Methods An extract of records from the Western Australian (WA) Hospital Morbidity Data Collection 2011–2015 and WA Death Registrations 2011–2015 were encoded to Bloom filters, and then linked using privacy-preserving methods. ### Results The PPRL method using Bloom filters provided similar linkage quality to the traditional un-encoded linkage, with 99.3% of ‘groupings’ identical between privacy preserving and clear-text linkage. Percentage of missing values in each field in the two datasets Open in a new tab a Increased to 0.1% after data cleaning b Increased to 0.1% after data cleaning ### Privacy preserving linkage approach The data was encoded for privacy preserving linkage using field-based Bloom filters; each identifier was encoded into a separate Bloom filter, with a standard probabilistic record linkage method used on these encoded identifiers. The same blocking strategy was used for the privacy preserving and clear-text linkages; this ensured that all differences in results reflected differences between encoded and non-encoded record comparison, rather than due to records which were simply not compared by one party.
